meta.title: Who really said "When the End of the World Comes, I Want To Be in Cincinnati. It Is Always Ten Years Behind the Times"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Shaw, and not Mark Twain. It is an anonymous German quip printed in 1886 about Bavaria; Cincinnati and Twain only turn up in the late 1970s.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'When the End of the World Comes, I Want To Be in Cincinnati. It Is Always Ten Years Behind the Times'?
meta.ogDescription: The joke travelled from Bavaria to Holland to Mecklenburg to Cincinnati, collecting a new famous name each time. Shaw's was attached in 1998.

answer.label: Not George Bernard Shaw — a travelling joke with no known author
answer.authorDates: In English print by October 1886 · originally about Bavaria, not Cincinnati
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator ↗ traces this quip to an anonymous German saying about Bavaria, printed in The Atlantic Monthly in October 1886 — long before anyone put Cincinnati, Mark Twain or Shaw in it. Shaw’s name is attached to only one variant, and only in 1998, when President Clinton told a Limerick audience ↗ that Shaw “hoped to be in Ireland on the day the world ended” — forty-eight years after Shaw died.

source.heading: Where the joke actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Bavaria — the end of the world would arrive there “fifty years later than in any other country”
First documented 1977–79, credited to Mark Twain, who died in 1910
Ireland, 50 years — the one Shaw citation on record is a 1998 speech by President Clinton

source.excerpt: It is a common saying in Germany that Bavaria will be the best place to emigrate to at the approaching end of the world, since that event, like everything else, will be sure to come off there fifty years later than in any other country. The Bavarians will be behind the times even as to the point when time shall be no more, and will enter as laggards upon the eternal life.
trail: 1886 — the oldest known form is anonymous and German. The Atlantic Monthly reports a common German saying that Bavaria is the place to be when the world ends, because the event will arrive there fifty years later than anywhere else (Quote Investigator ↗). A version in German almost certainly predates it.

1963–1976 — the joke starts collecting famous names as it moves around the map: Heinrich Heine and Holland from 1963, Otto von Bismarck and Mecklenburg in 1969, James Boswell and the Netherlands in a 1976 New York Times piece. Each name was attached long after the man had died (chronology ↗).

1977–1979 — Cincinnati and Mark Twain appear for the first time, in a University of Houston keynote address and then in a scholarly article that flags the line “probably apocryphal” in the same sentence it prints it. The University of Cincinnati’s own archivist is blunter: “Twain never said it” ↗.

1998 — Shaw’s name finally enters, and not about Cincinnati at all. Speaking in Limerick, President Clinton says Shaw “hoped to be in Ireland on the day the world ended” because the Irish ran fifty years behind (American Presidency Project ↗). Will Rogers is credited by 2004.
source.excerptNote: E. P. Evans, “A Mad Monarch,” The Atlantic Monthly, October 1886 — the article begins on page 449 and this passage falls on page 452 — as transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗. No Cincinnati, no ten years, and no named author: Evans presents it simply as a common saying.

sourceLink.text: Quote Investigator: the full chronology, 1886 to 2004

source.rightsNote: The Cincinnati wording cannot be tied to any identified work. Its earliest known printings — a conference volume published in 1978 and a 1979 journal article — are modern, in-copyright publications, and neither presents itself as quoting a document. The 1886 Atlantic Monthly ancestor is long out of copyright, but it is a different sentence, about Bavaria, by an unnamed originator, so quotle.info asserts no public-domain status for the line as it circulates today.

author.name: George Bernard Shaw
author.heading: So where does Shaw come into it?
author.metaLine: 1856–1950 · Irish playwright, critic and Nobel laureate
author.bio: Born in Dublin in 1856 and dead in Hertfordshire in 1950, Shaw wrote more than sixty plays and worked for years as a theatre and music critic, political activist and professional provocateur. He took the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1925 and later became the first person to hold both a Nobel and an Academy Award. He was quotable enough that stray lines drift toward him by gravity — but this one reached him only in 1998, forty-eight years after his death, and in a form about Ireland rather than Cincinnati.

Quote Investigator traces it to an anonymous German saying printed in The Atlantic Monthly in October 1886, where the place was Bavaria and the lag was fifty years. Cincinnati and Mark Twain appear only in the late 1970s; Shaw's name is attached to an Ireland version only in 1998, when President Clinton quoted it in a speech at Limerick — forty-eight years after Shaw died. — Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: Six famous names, none of them supported
misattribution.intro: This is a joke that swaps its target city and its famous author roughly every decade. At least six names have been attached to it, and Quote Investigator ↗ finds no compelling evidence for any of them.

items.why: Shaw appears in the record exactly once, in President Clinton’s remarks at Limerick on 5 September 1998 ↗ — and the place is Ireland, not Cincinnati. Shaw died on 2 November 1950 (Wikipedia ↗), forty-eight years earlier, and the line appears nowhere on his Wikiquote page ↗.

Twain died in 1910, and the first Cincinnati telling documented by Quote Investigator ↗ is a keynote address given in 1977 and printed the following year. When a scholarly journal ran the line in 1979 it was already labelled “probably apocryphal.” The University of Cincinnati archives put it plainly: the statement “arose in the 1970s” with no documentation ↗.

items.who: Heinrich Heine and Otto von Bismarck
items.why: Heine is the first famous name ever attached, in a 1963 broadcasting review that has him sending everyone to Holland, where things happen fifty years late; Heine had died in 1856. Bismarck gets Mecklenburg in a 1969 periodical, with the lag shrunk to two years, and again in a 1975 New York Times letter with fifty (Quote Investigator ↗).

A 1976 New York Times story hands the Netherlands version to Boswell; by 2004 a book of one-liners has the Cincinnati version under Will Rogers’s name. Both are late arrivals in a chain that runs back to 1886 ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer is that nobody knows who made the joke. It was already circulating anonymously in Germany before 1886, and every famous name on it — Shaw included — was added long afterwards, usually decades after the supposed speaker had died (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: A joke that keeps moving house
lead: Some quotations are stolen; this one is more like a rental property. The structure never changes — when the world ends, go to X, because everything arrives there N years late — while the city, the lag and the wit who supposedly said it are all swapped out to suit whoever is telling it. Bavaria and fifty years in 1886. Dresden in 1910. Holland under Heine’s name from the 1960s. Mecklenburg under Bismarck’s, once with the lag cut to a mere two years. Then Cincinnati and ten years, under Mark Twain’s.

That churn is exactly what makes the attribution worthless. A genuine quotation has a fixed wording and a document behind it. This one has neither: the wording is whatever the joke needs, and the earliest witness, an 1886 magazine article, explicitly presents it as something everybody in Germany already says. Shaw’s name arrived at the very end of the chain, in a 1998 political speech, applied to a version about Ireland that has nothing to do with Cincinnati at all.
detailsBody: Twain really did have a Cincinnati connection — he worked in the city as a young printer in the 1850s, which is the hook local retellings hang the quip on. But a plausible biography is not evidence. The line surfaces more than sixty years after his death, and the scholar who first printed it in an academic journal in 1979 flagged it as probably apocryphal on the spot.

The wording on this page, with “ten years behind the times,” matches that 1979 journal transcription. The version that circulates most widely online says twenty years instead. Both are modern, and neither can be traced to anything Twain wrote.
context.pull: Every generation gives the joke a new city and a new author.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator traces the joke to an anonymous German saying printed in The Atlantic Monthly, October 1886 (E. P. Evans, 'A Mad Monarch', start page 449, quote page 452) about Bavaria being fifty years behind; lists Heine/Holland from 1963, Bismarck/Mecklenburg 1969 and 1975, Boswell/Netherlands 1976, Twain/Cincinnati from a 1977 University of Houston keynote printed in 1978, the 'ten years behind the times' wording in a 1979 American Literary Realism article calling it 'probably apocryphal', Clinton crediting Shaw in 1998, and Will Rogers by 2004; and concludes there is no compelling evidence the joke was crafted by Twain, Heine, Bismarck, Shaw, Boswell or Rogers.

In Remarks in Limerick, Ireland on September 5, 1998, President Clinton said: 'George Bernard Shaw once quipped that he hoped to be in Ireland on the day the world ended, because the Irish were always 50 years behind the times.'

The University of Cincinnati Archives and Rare Books Library states that Twain never said the Cincinnati line, that 'the spurious statement arose in the 1970s' and that there has never been any documentation of him uttering or penning those words.
No version of the end-of-the-world / behind-the-times line appears anywhere on Wikiquote's George Bernard Shaw page (checked 1 Sep 2026).

George Bernard Shaw was born 26 July 1856 in Dublin and died 2 November 1950 in Ayot St Lawrence; he was a playwright, theatre and music critic, political activist and polemicist, wrote more than sixty plays, won the 1925 Nobel Prize in Literature and was the first person to win both a Nobel Prize and an Academy Award.

Internet Archive item sim_atlantic_1886-10_58_348 is The Atlantic Monthly, October 1886, Volume 58, Issue 348 — the issue Quote Investigator cites for the earliest known printing. The scan itself is lending-restricted, so the passage could not be read there directly.
